title: Experts question police tactics in killing of Truro man
article: A former police chief and expert in non-physical intervention is questioning why the province isn't calling a formal inquiry into the fatal police shooting of Bradley Clattenburg last May.

"All the provinces I know do this automatically when a person is killed by a police action, whether it's in custody, or following a shooting or car pursuit, the matter automatically goes to a provincial inquest," said Terry Coleman, who's given expert testimony in several police inquiries and inquests involving civilians who have died as a result of police shootings.
Clattenburg was armed with a loaded sawed off shotgun when three police officers opened fire on the 24-year-old during the morning hours of May 26 in Westphal.

Coleman said he's surprised the SiRT report does not delve into whether crisis de-escalation strategies were considered or used by police before the fatal exchange. In fact, he said, the report demonstrates officers may have been too aggressive in attempting to disarm Clattenburg. "What I notice and it is a really big no-no is that all three officers were yelling at this man at the same time," said Coleman. The report states that officers followed and eventually cornered Clattenburg while he had the shotgun pointed under his chin, repeatedly shouting at Clattenburg to drop his weapon.
Clattenburg eventually lowered the weapon and pointed it at two of the officers, which is when all three officers fired.

Coleman - who has 40 years of policing-related experience, including 27 years as a Calgary officer, and a six-year stint as chief in Moose Jaw - says the officers' deadly actions could have been justified and it might have been impossible for them to communicate with Clattenburg. But there are lingering questions, he says, including whether two of the officers needed to be armed with carbines. He also questions whether officers attempted to diffuse the situation by providing Clattenburg more space and time to calm down.

"Sometimes the best thing to do is to try to contain the area as best as you can and back up. You can still contain the area, find a safe position that might be behind the engine block of a vehicle and call for more assistance.
"Police could have moved too fast. At the point where he has the gun pointed at himself he's not threatening anyone but himself. You're yelling drop your weapon, there's something wrong with that."

The Chronicle Herald's attempts to reach SiRT director Felix Cacchione were unsuccessful. Justice Minister Mark Furey also couldn't be reached for comment. Department spokeswoman Heather Fairbairn wouldn't comment on whether the case warranted an inquest or on the details of the investigation, saying Cacchione has the resources and legislative authority to conduct investigations as he deems appropriate.

The SiRT report says that both Halifax Regional Police and RCMP officers attended the scene but neither department would say which officers were involved in the shooting or how many officers arrived at the scene.

The Herald inquired with the RCMP and HRP to find out if officers at the scene attempted to use non-violent techniques to disarm Clattenburg and whether the officers had any mental health intervention training. John MacLeod, spokesman for HRP, said he couldn't comment since the police investigation has been handled by RCMP. RCMP provided no response.

Coleman, who trains officers across the country in de-escalation techniques, says many police departments aren't adequately equipped to deal with crisis situations involving people with serious mental health issues. He says the amount and quality of training officers receive varies greatly from province to province. In many crisis cases officers resort to a standard but aggressive "command and control response," says Coleman.
"What's missing is a serious effort to hammer home de-escalation. Because what you practise and what you have been trained to do all along is what will stick with you."

Sheila Wildeman, a Dalhousie University law professor, says she's also surprised that the SiRT report failed to show whether crisis de-escalation strategies were considered or used by police. Wildeman, an expert in disability and human rights law, said the review ought to have looked at what might have been done to prevent what she calls Clattenburg's tragic death.

Like Coleman, Wildeman says the case might warrant a provincial inquiry under the Fatality Investigations Act that could draw conclusions about the circumstances and manner of Clattenburg's death, "but also to make recommendations about how Nova Scotia's mental health, policing, and social support systems may be strengthened so that such tragic deaths may be prevented in future."

Wildeman says alternatively, the province's justice minister could order an independent investigation relating to policing, under section 7 of the Police Act. Under that section, the minister may set terms of reference which, she says, could include inquiries into whether crisis intervention strategies were applied or could have been applied to avert the lethal use of force in this case.

According to the SiRT report, police received a 911 from a woman saying Clattenburg arrived at her home with a firearm, threatening to kill her son. She also said that Clattenburg was most likely suffering from some mental health issues and that he had accused her son of planting an audio chip in his head, which enabled him to hear his girlfriend having sex with different men. The 911 call was registered at 7:48 a.m. Less than two hours later, at 9:22 a.m., RCMP contacted SiRT to report the fatal shooting.
Wildeman says there's a number of questions that ought to be answered in the SiRT report.

"The 911 call had informed police that the individual posing a threat in the home was experiencing significant mental health problems. How if at all did this affect the police response? What if any actions did police take to de-escalate the situation? Was contact made with the Mental Health Mobile Crisis Team? Did the RCMP and (HRP) officers on the scene have mental health crisis intervention training? Assuming that they did, how did they use that training?"
The mandate of SiRT is to decide whether criminal charges should be laid against police. But Wildeman says the report ought to demonstrate whether Clattenburg's death could have been prevented.

"The question of what if any opportunities there were for crisis de-escalation should be front of mind for all of us - police, health professionals, legal professionals - whenever a person in mental health crisis is deemed to be presenting a risk to their own safety or that of others."
